title_en: Spot and fix: fallacies and hidden assumptions
title_he: לזהות ולתקן: כשלים לוגיים והנחות סמויות

instructions.en: The illustrative paragraph below argues for a school phone ban. Its conclusion may be reasonable, but almost every step that leads to it is weak. Each item quotes one sentence from it: find what is wrong with the reasoning, then choose or complete a repair that a careful writer could defend. The aim is to fix the argument, not to collect fallacy names, and the same checks apply to your own drafts.

input_text:
Illustrative paragraph (invented for this task; the school and the town are fictional).

(1) Since Ardenvale High banned phones in March, its exam results have risen, so the ban clearly caused the improvement. (2) Every teacher I have spoken to supports the ban, which shows that phones are harmful to all students. (3) Opponents of the ban are mostly teenagers who simply want to play games in class. (4) If students keep their phones, they will text during lessons, then stop listening altogether, and soon nobody will be able to concentrate on anything. (5) Either we ban phones completely, or we admit that schools have given up on discipline. (6) After all, no one has ever proved that phones help anyone learn. (7) The town's other schools should therefore copy Ardenvale's ban at once.

scaffold.en: Cause: Did anything else change? How exactly would X produce Y?
Sample: How many cases are there, and are they typical of the group the claim is about?
Opponents: Would they accept this description of their view?
Chains and choices: Which step has evidence? Are there really only two options?
Hidden links: What must be true, but is not said, for the conclusion to follow?

checklist.en: For every causal claim, I ask what else could explain the result and say how the cause would work.
My sample is large and representative enough for the size of my claim, or I narrow the claim.
I describe opponents' views in terms they would accept, and I answer their strongest argument.
I test every "either... or", "will lead to", "no one has proved" and "everyone" in my own drafts.
I can name the unstated assumption that links my evidence to my conclusion, and I check that it holds.

items.question: Sentence 1: "Since Ardenvale High banned phones in March, its exam results have risen, so the ban clearly caused the improvement." Which question exposes the weakness in this reasoning?
options: How many students at Ardenvale High own a phone, and how many brought it to lessons before March?
Did anything else change at the school that year, such as staff, timetables or the exams themselves?
Do the teachers at Ardenvale High support the ban, and would they like other schools to copy it?
Are exam results the best measure of a school's success, or should well-being count as well?

explanation.en: Results rising after the ban does not show that the ban caused the rise (post hoc, or false cause). The writer would need to rule out other changes and explain how a ban would raise results.

items.question: Which revision of sentence 1 ("Since Ardenvale High banned phones in March, its exam results have risen, so the ban clearly caused the improvement.") claims only what the evidence supports?
options: Since Ardenvale High banned phones in March, its results have risen, which proves beyond any reasonable doubt that the ban worked.
Ardenvale High's results have nothing to do with the phone ban, since exam results go up and down every year anyway.
Everyone knows that results rise when phones are banned, and Ardenvale High's rise since March is simply the latest example.
Ardenvale High's results rose after the March ban; the ban may have helped, but other changes that year must be ruled out first.

0.en: Stronger, not better: "proves beyond doubt" over-claims even more.

1.en: This over-corrects: the evidence does not show that there is no link either.

explanation.en: The repaired version keeps the observation, offers the causal link only as a possibility ("may have helped") and names what would have to be checked.

prompt.en: Match each sentence from the paragraph to the question that would repair it.

pairs: (2) Every teacher I have spoken to supports the ban, which shows that phones are harmful to all students.
How many cases is this, are they typical, and is support for a ban evidence of harm?
(3) Opponents of the ban are mostly teenagers who simply want to play games in class.
Would opponents accept this description? What is their strongest argument?
(4) If students keep their phones, they will text during lessons, then stop listening altogether, and soon nobody will be able to concentrate on anything.
Which step in this chain has evidence, and which is only assumed?
(5) Either we ban phones completely, or we admit that schools have given up on discipline.
Are there other options, such as limits on when phones may be used?
(6) After all, no one has ever proved that phones help anyone learn.
Does a lack of proof that phones help count as proof that they harm?

explanation.en: Each repair question targets one weak step: a small, unrepresentative sample of opinions (2), a caricature of the other side (3), a chain of consequences with no evidence for its links (4), a false choice between two options (5), and treating absence of proof as proof of the opposite (6).

prompt.en: Replace the straw man in sentence 3.

items.question: Sentence 3 dismisses opponents as "teenagers who simply want to play games in class". Which objection should the paragraph answer instead, because it is the strongest case the other side could make?
options: Teenagers enjoy games on their phones, and taking the phones away for the school day will make them resentful.
Phones are expensive and easily lost or broken, so most students would be better off leaving them at home.
Phones can support learning, through quick research or class apps, and parents may need to reach their children.
Teachers who support the ban are simply too strict and do not understand how young people communicate today.

explanation.en: Answering the strongest version of the opposing view makes the argument more convincing; answering a caricature (a straw man) persuades only readers who already agree. Calling teachers "too strict" just attacks the other side in return.

items.question: Sentence 2: "Every teacher I have spoken to supports the ban, which shows that phones are harmful to all students." Which revision claims only what this evidence can support?
options: The teachers I have spoken to support the ban, which suggests that at least some staff see phones as a distraction in lessons.
Every teacher in the country supports the ban, which shows clearly that phones are harmful to all students everywhere.
Most of the teachers I have spoken to support the ban, so phones must be harmful to most of their students.
Some of the teachers I have spoken to support the ban, which proves that phones harm at least some students.

1.en: This widens the sample without evidence and keeps the leap from opinion to harm.

2.en: "Most" is smaller than "all", but teachers' support is still treated as proof of harm.

3.en: "Some" does not repair a sentence that still treats opinion as proof.

explanation.en: The evidence is the opinions of an unknown number of teachers the writer happens to know. It supports a claim about those teachers' views, not a claim that phones harm every student (hasty generalisation).

items.question: Sentence 5 offers only two options: "Either we ban phones completely, or we admit that schools have given up on discipline." Which revision removes the false choice?
options: Either we ban phones completely, or classrooms will descend into chaos and teachers will lose control of lessons.
Schools could ban phones, allow them only at break, or allow them for set tasks, and should compare the results.
We must ban phones completely, because there is no other way to protect lessons from constant interruption.
Either we ban phones completely, or discipline will slowly get worse, year by year, until it is lost altogether.

explanation.en: The repair names the options between the two extremes and proposes a way to choose among them. The other versions keep a two-option frame, or simply declare that no other option exists.

prompt.en: Find the unstated assumption in sentence 7.

items.question: Sentence 7: "The town's other schools should therefore copy Ardenvale's ban at once." Which unstated assumption must hold for this conclusion to follow?
options: That the other schools are similar enough to Ardenvale High for a ban to work the same way.
That the other schools in the town already have some kind of phone ban in place.
That most teachers at the town's other schools are currently opposed to a ban.
That Ardenvale High's exam results had been falling steadily in the years before March.

1.en: If they already had a ban, there would be nothing to copy.

2.en: The conclusion does not depend on what teachers at other schools think.

3.en: The argument does not need this: it claims only that results rose after March.

explanation.en: To move from "it worked here" to "do it everywhere", the writer silently assumes the other schools are alike in the ways that matter: students, rules, and the reasons for their results. Stating the assumption shows what evidence is missing, such as results from comparable schools or a trial before a town-wide rule.

prompt.en: Repair sentence 6 ("After all, no one has ever proved that phones help anyone learn."). Complete the new version with one word so that it no longer treats a lack of proof as proof.

items.text: Even if no study has shown that phones help students learn, that alone does not ___ that phones harm learning.

feedback.en: "Disprove" reverses the meaning. The point is that missing evidence for one claim does not establish the opposite claim.

hint.en: Which verb links evidence to a conclusion: "this does not ___ that..."?

explanation.en: Absence of evidence for one claim (phones help) is not evidence for the opposite claim (phones harm). A defensible writer either supplies evidence of harm or limits the conclusion.
